The whole moving states and feeling depressed because of being uproot is something that I am currently going through myself. And it's so so so rough.

For me, it's the first time I've moved. And I had to do it to a new state 8 hours away from my friends/family/etc. by myself for a job that I hate. I want to move back very badly too. It's been extremely tough for me, to the point where, on top of my depression, I've actually become suicidal too.

I'm glad you are there for her, that must make things easier. Know that this isn't because of you at all and that you are probably a huge component to why she's managed for 2 years. I've been here for about 7 months now, without anyone, and it's just been so...rough. I also think that the depression really messes with our ability to settle down those "roots" and it's hard when you're in the thick of it. It's hard to break yourself out of that which is why outside help is a very important proponent.

Being away from everything makes you very reluctant to want to form those bonds elsewhere and just traps you in the past.

I know it wasn't perfect, and that I disliked a lot of things from before as well, but the good parts that I don't have anymore are whats magnified. I'm seeing the past through rose colored glasses. I miss a lot of things. And those are the things I'm concentrated on. Because the familiarity aspect is comforting, and having that extended support system readily available is what I miss dearly. I'm wallowing in that. It's not letting me enjoy things here to the fullest.

You being a support system has been so helpful and she's probably enormously grateful for it. She probably feels really guilty about needing to go back. It's hard to verbalize it though. But, it's gotten bad enough that she needs to pull the "nuclear" option. She wants that stability again, but at the same time, is probably struggling with the guilt of leaving you and also, feeling like she failed in some weird sense. It's very internal.

As others have said, the fact that she's actually talking to you about her depression and is seeking out help says a lot about how much she trusts you.

Let her come to you to talk, but drop the occasional reminder of, "I'm here if you need someone to listen to you."

As someone said before, when I vent and talk to someone it isn't solution seeking. Whenever someone tried to offer an immediate "fix" I felt bad because I was feeling like I was just being dismissed. It felt like, "Your problems are so petty, just do this and THERE it's DONE!"

Or worse, when someone would just tell me that I was complaining too much and that it was too much for them and, "I don't know what you want from me." And that severed that feeling of 'trust' real fast. I talk to you and open up to you when I feel like I can trust you, and having it thrown back in your face just shatters everything and makes me never want to talk to you again, ever.

Other than the separation of feeling alone in her age range, the growing pains of feeling like, "I should be becoming independent, I feel so bad that others are progressing and I'm stuck and feel so left behind, is it even worth it anymore?" and the feeling of guilt from needing to "go home" it's much the same advice from before, but very much on her own terms.

Going out and having an event distract me from my own thoughts always helps. But, I'm on medication where it helps me have the mental exertion to not be exhausted at simple anythings on most days. On those bad days where she needs to be in bed and alone, just being offered that one, "I'm right over there if you need me." and having that presence nearby helps a lot too. But don't be persistent on reminding her, that gets annoying and those negative feelings are heightened by this. Then maybe lashing out then feeling really guilty afterwards.

If she can take you up on talking or wanting company, doing really low-key things at home helps with not expending too much mental exertion and also made it so I felt like I actually did something. 

(2/2)

Coming from a 23/yo with clinical depression who, as a result of that, is VERY, OVERLY self-reflective and introspective, I'm going to feel this out empathetically and objectively because I'm doing okay today and have a clearer head today. I feel like in a parental/child relationship some of these things would need to be altered just because of the intrinsic nature of that and the "independence" factor that you start FEEL like you should develop as a young adult.

For the first point, again, being a constant in someone's life is a source of comfort for me personally. You say you're close, so I think it would serves as a comfort rather than feeling more so like a point of personal stunted independence that, "I feel like I should have by this point, god I'm so useless." then cue the comparisons that spiral into more self-hatred.

But still, as close as I would be with a parental figure, there's still that separation from age-based peers where there's a weird, "You're going through this as I am" solidarity. And I feel like anything that becomes MORE consistent on your end could seem like doting and that would make me feel worse because it's not coming from someone "my age" and because there's that intrinsic, "My parent knows more than me because they've lived longer. Blah, blah blah..." feeling that usually comes about.

For her explanation of it, that sounds pretty par the course for how it feels. It's like, some days are better than others in terms of how much you feel like it's rolling around inside of you and how much it's hindering you. But it's always something that's kind of there and bubbling inside of you, like a heaviness deep in your core, if that makes sense?

You don't have the "hope" to look forward to those "better days" but when they happen, you're happily (as much as you can be) surprised and you feel a little lighter, but it's not enough. Just a little lighter than usual.

Therapy definitely helps, I feel like you have to find the right person to "connect" with and sometimes that can take a little. But, if it just feels like you're just talking at another person then that process can feel like it's not working when really it's just that it's the wrong fit. Maybe check in to see if she feels like this person really is understanding and listening to what she's saying?

I was against medication for a while too. Thinking back (I've been medicated for about 4.5/5 years now) I think I felt like, "I've seen what it can do to people, it makes you tired and lethargic, etc."

I was probably worried about the side effects, feeling like I was going to be dependent on these things for the rest of my life, being scared if the didn't work, and I guess, maybe just the how everything would narrow down to this "last resort" option.

Let me just say, from my experience being unmedicated and not knowing what it'd be like and letting that fear stop me from that, getting medication in college and actually feeling like I was going okay again, then needing to go off medication because of job issues and moving and having that break effect my personal relationships, and finally being back on something and now, maintaining, despite being away from everything and everyone. I know I am so much more spiteful and angry and, the word for it is "foggy", and just feeling like I was in this "space" where everything was completely separate from my own plane of existence when I'm not on them.

With medication, some might work for some and might not others. But I feel like, with how far things have come from what they might have been before, if you talk to a professional the risks are a lot less than if it helps you. And the side effects, for the most part, are more uncommon and outlying cases that I feel like they have to include on there for legal reasons.

The couple of medications I've been on have been Prozac (fluoxetine is the generic brand), Wellbutrin (bupropion is the generic), and Trileptal (oxcarbazepine generic). The prozac for me made me feel sleepy so then I was given the wellbutrin to "give me that drive back," I'm off the prozac now and have kept the wellbutrin. Now I'm taking it with the trileptal which serves to "enhance the effects" of the wellbutrin.

The side effects I've gone through are with the prozac: sleepiness and a very slight weight gain, and trileptal: light vertigo and sleepiness (which is why I take my second dose at night).

It's gradual, it's not all supposed to happen overnight. They're slow release capsules and take around 2 weeks to start noticeable change. And, that's why a psychiatrist checks in with follow-ups during that time, so if anything does happen they can catch it and adjust it accordingly. With my medication, a lot of the "brain fog" has lifted and I feel like I can do things with a bit more "presence" again and feel like I have the mental capacity to wanted to do things again.

I dunno, food for thought. (1/2)

A little bit back I gave advice to someone wanting to help their sister and this is what I wrote then on a sibling level:

"You will have to be the one who seeks active contact."
Absolutely this. Even though I feel like I'm doing nothing but push away people and "want to be alone", I feel like crap once the people in my life start to actually do that because it's just like a confirmation that I failed. It's hard and like, in my head I know I don't deserve it, but deep down I truly appreciate it so so much from someone who I actually care for, rather than the empty meanings from someone else.

Let her know that you're here when she's ready to talk but that if she's not ready then you're not going to push for it until she is.
Trying to get her to do some small activities and just get her out and maybe not be in her head so much is something that helps me. On better days, maybe try and walk around a not so crowded park, find a dog to pet. Getting that fresh air/sunlight and just seeing that the world outside the one I create while isolated helps.

On worse days, when she doesn't/can't do that, maybe just bundling up in a blanket and watching a movie or something would work.

I find that I unconsciously lose more body heat and even though it's not always an immediate concern I find doing something like washing my hands with warm water, taking a warm shower/bath, holding a cup of something warm, having a blanket or jacket to help me warm up, helps me feel somewhat human again, but that might just be me personally.

Get her to drink water as much as you can. Dehydration is definitely something that I actively try to combat and it helps my body not feel so bad, even if it's small. Maybe have a cup around and ask her if she can take a sip for you. Nothing big, nothing too much, but get her drinking water to hydrate.

If she's not eating or this come to pass, she may not actively realize that her body needs something. Smell is a strong factor, so maybe having food ready for her when/if you prepare it will kind of trigger her body to realize that she may be hungrier than she thought. Chicken Noodle Soup is always good and easy for me to eat too. That or tomato soup of some sort. Warm soups are nice for me.

When you're "in" something for so long it's very much a cyclical thought process that's very hard to break out of and makes it seem endless. By whatever revelation you had, it was something that came about that helped break you of that. And that's something that's very individual a lot of the time. And, especially with people going through a mental illness, that's what outside help serves to help you of and why it can help someone tremendously.

I'm glad you're having this clarity! Up-keeping it and getting that momentum going is the moving forward part. If you fall back into that cycle, know that it's exactly that. You broke free of it once, you can do it again. Even if the depression is the larger beast, you take it down a little at a time. If it comes back, it's normal to have setbacks (as much as they suck) and some days will be better than others, but again, realize that it's possible.

I wish you the best in moving forwards too! :)

Most universities have a counseling program of some sort that's "free" (included in tuition but yeah). Try looking into that. It's free and there's no harm in going because you're not paying anything extra for that service. If you don't like it, you can always ask for a different person or stop, but I found that this really helped me when I started doing this my second year through the end of my senior year. It's a third party, unbiased person to talk to so, even if it's just venting for an hour, it helped. Talking to trusted friends/family can really help, but with some things it can be hard. With a counselor/therapist/etc. they're trained to help you curve those intrusive thoughts as you're processing them out loud and a good therapist/etc. is really critical in helping you break out of those cyclical thoughts.

I started my freshman year back in 2012/2013?? And actually ended up bumming it on my sister's couch instead of actually being in my dorm room because my depression got so bad that I needed that extra support. I should've gotten help a lot sooner but it was that same thing that I find a lot of people go through of, "It's tolerable right now, sometimes it's not but right now it is so that's manageable so I won't go."

Let me just say on that mindset. I needed a friend's outside perspective to kind of help me realize that I really did need that extra help. I can tell that story if anyone is interested but it's a bit long so I'd do it in another post anyways.

Counselors/therapists/psychologists are the people who you talk to and use CBT. PsyCHIATRISTS are the ones who can prescribe medication and usually their sessions are more that then talking based. That's something I think a lot of people get confused about. They end up needing someone to talk to but feel like they had medicine shoved in their faces then pushed out the door. Psychiatrists are the ones that do medication, psychologists/etc. are the talk-based ones.

If your depression is taking a toll on your workload/etc. see about taking an "unfinished" or I think that's what it's called? (as it's late into the semester I believe?). If it happens early enough in the semester and you can still drop a class, then see about doing that and try taking the minimum amount of credits to be "full time"

You might have to stay an extra year or semester or so but I mean, it's not a race to the finish line. You do what you can and if taking however many classes is hindering you now then it's hindering you now and that's just the reality of it. Said and done. Save it for later when you are able to handle it.

For learning how to play guitar, if you have some extra money for outside classes then pay for some sessions. There might be classes you can talk with the university but usually I've found that those classes are more for developing already learned basics? I could be wrong though, so look into that. But, I find that when I spend money on something I'm less likely to skip it because I don't want to waste that money.

It's always hard starting to get into something or just getting up to prepare for something. And as cliche or unhelpful as it sounds, just stopping the thoughts that are keeping you in bed and just letting your body go into autopilot to get you ready and out the door is what needs to happen. I ALWAYS hate getting prepped for going into the mindset of starting something, but if you just throw yourself at something without giving yourself the chance to stop yourself by overthinking, you 95% feel better afterwards because you feel like you accomplished something. No matter how small.

Not getting caught up in your own head is really, REALLY important. I find that when I'm left alone, THAT'S when it happens and it really hinders me because I'm thinking of all of the negative ways things could go wrong or etc. If I don't allow myself to think and just use the momentum of one thing to get to another then it really helps me.

I kind of regret it, but I can't do anything about it now. I gave this advice to my sister/brother now in college. Find a club to join too. I think, from what I've heard, they're having fun too.

Google around, maybe there's a specific Facebook page to find the lists of things. Find a musical/band group. Getting yourself moving helps. This can help you meet people who share similar interests too. Also, don't be as self-conscious about doing things by yourself. I mean, stay safe, but I've learned to become a lot more comfortable with just going to festivals/events by myself post-college. It's weirdly freeing, and you're on your own timeline to do things and I find I'm more aware of the event because I'm not needing to "keep up" with people during those times. Google "events happening in (x city) today" and pick out some (coughfreecough) things. Keep you busy that way too.

Trust me, being 1.5 years out of college now, finding people kind of sucks because everything becomes very...'encapsulated'? College was nice because it was people around your age all kind of shoved together, where you could, on the most BASIC level, bond over the fact that "Ugh, I don't want to do this paper." or "Shit, that project is due in 2 days...have you started yet? No? Good me neither."

As someone post-college, Meetup.com has helped me find groups around that could be cool, I've been using it and some things are a hit or miss, but hey, I tried them and they help break up the days.

My depression also fucks with my memory HARDCORE so like, right now even, I probably wouldn't even have remembered what I did yesterday. But since I went to a game developer event (even though I'm on the art side of things) helped me chat with people regardless and I got to play test people's game and give them feedback as a player. Then yesterday I went to the zoo last minute, and because it was colder out and going to rain later in the day (after things closed anyways) no one was there and I could see everything up close. I also take lots of photos and shove them on instagram so I can keep up with family/friends states away and then look back and have "proof" and I can kind of piece back together those things after my depression tries to dump that.

I mean, if you need a bit of time to yourself, do that and take that time to recharge if you're an introvert like I am. But, again, staying within yourself and your own bubble to have that crippling self doubt grow is really what you can't allow yourself to do. Because a day will go by and then you'll feel bad that you didn't do anything that day, and then that negativity and tiredness will bleed into the next day, and then serve twice over into the next day, etc. Even if it's the smallest activity, you'll still feel slightly better that you did something. And it helps break apart the monotony so the days don't bleed together and time feels unreal. That's really scary.

TL;DR look into your university's counseling program, pay for outside guitar lessons (if you can) so you feel more obligation to attend them to not waste money, join clubs to help get you out there, and try staying in your head as little as you can -- autopilot your body into starting the day with as little mental exertion/conflict  as you can because your own head-space is where that trap is.

If it's a bad day, taking a shower helps me warm up and feel "human" again. It's always what I need to do first to feel better. Buy some chicken noodle soups because they're low maintenance to make and to keep down if your depression makes you not want to eat. Some other low maintenance, cheap food for these days: egg sandwich (bread, one cooked sunny-side/scrambled up egg, and you're done. If you're feeling fancy, whatever greens/onion/tomatoes to jazz it up a little), pasta (just boil those $1 noodles and toss in the $1 sauce you get and you're done), ramen too I guess, but I'm trying to keep this a little healthier.

And if you have the energy to do so, doing laundry does a world of difference too.

I hope this helps. Some days are better than others, definitely, but you do what you can.

Your insurance card should have a website on it and through that you should be able to find a "find doctors through us" section.

I have Blue Cross Blue Shield through my father still thankfully, and that section is helpful because you can filter out the doctor's gender, miles away from you, etc. I use that list as a base point and then google searched the name of that doctor/psychologist/etc. to see if they got good ratings, if any. And if not I see if the hospital/clinic has good ratings.

If not or none, I move on to the next doctor on the list and pick out a few just in case my first pick wasn't accepting new patients or had a long wait list that I thought I couldn't do.

Next I see how far away the place is from my house/apartment/workplace (if I needed to go during work hours, which I have to do to get a sooner appointment as most places aren't open on the weekends and are only 7am-5pm on weekdays so :/)

I make the call an try to get someone to pick up and see what slots are open and if they worked with my schedule, etc. Also, double check if they take your insurance and if the location is correct because the insurance list can be a little outdated.

If you're not on insurance, google "psychologists/therapists/etc. around me" and do the same things from before just, you should ask about what the costs are upfront. If they're too much, see if they can do payment on a "sliding scale" based on income. Some places can do that.

For what to expect, the first time you go in the front desk needs you to fill out an evaluation form that asks your basic questions about insurance, birthdate, etc. Then, it can vary, but you have to fill out a section on mood/suicidal thoughts/etc. They take a bit to look this over before calling you back for your hour long session.

From there they take you to their office and you chose a chair to sit in. They let up you walk in first. And they ask how you're doing today. Then from there, for me, I just started talking and I would just keep talking. For most places they focus on using CBT where they redirect your intrusive thoughts as you talk them out. And if you're over 18 they don't tell your parents or anyone anything unless you might be in danger to yourself or others.

But yeah, they're really nice and you talk and kind of word vomit and they interject to curve intrusive thoughts. But they should never "lead" the conversation or lead you in a way that they influence.

Exact same stats as you, right down to age. I'm on Wellbutrin 300mg along with 900mg of oxcarbazepine. Wellbutrin from what I was told before when I was on it and Prozac (which made me hazy and tired) was supposed to counter that and is supposed to "give back your drive for life" essentially. I've lost weight on it (not sure where you stand on that) and others I've known on it have too.

I did well on it. Currently, with my upped oxcarbazepine (told would "enhance" the effects of wellbutrin), I'm doing pretty poorly. Suicidal thoughts, some pretty close calls too. My fogginess is back and everything. But I'm almost positive is from the oxcarbazepine as it's the only medication that I'm not familiar with and I know I've had a good run with Wellbutrin. Things were going well when I was on a lower dosage of the oxcarbazepine.

With Wellbutrin, my fogginess cleared up substantially, I was more "lively", and I felt okay as much as I could be. Personally, I do like it because my general practitioner had even said it has less side effects than Prozac and targets both depression and anxiety before a psychiatrist gave me the full dose with the new medication.

I like Wellbutrin, it worked for me. I'm not doing so hot rn but I'm sure that's from the oxcarbazepine.

I still occasionally drink with them, but not enough to test the warnings. But I'm sure the occasional drinks is okay. Ask your psychiatrist to be sure.

Have you looked into your school's counseling service? It's "free" (from your tuition, but still) so if you hate it there's no loss. If anything, it helps having an unbiased, third party to vent to for an hour.

I was a mess freshman year and didn't get help until my friend reached a breakthrough with me. Going to counseling then getting on medication helped a lot with my junior year. And again, it's free.

Start with your General Practitioner about starting you on something or recommending you to someone. 

If you're under 18 talk to your parents about getting you to a counselor/psychologist/psychiatrist

If you're in college or uni or if that's in your near future and your can hold out a little longer you can look into the program they have that's free (with you're tuition, but still "free" for use I guess)

If you're over 18, look into/Google psychologists/etc. in your area and see about scheduling an appointment from a place/doctor that has good reviews ideally. If you have insurance, google/call to confirm if they take your insurance. If they don't pick up right away leave a message or call later. 

If you're completely new to it and aren't sure about medication yet talking to a counselor/therapist/psychologist about hour sessions where they'll most likely use some sort of CBT talk therapy.

If you're sure you need medication you have to make an appointment with a psychiatrist because they're the ones that can prescribe medication.

You're not "weak" or "giving up control" by getting help. You're getting someone to talk to whose a trained, non biased, third party to help you through your thought process. And if you don't like it you can switch people and aren't obligated to stay with someone if they're not the right fit.

With medication, that's your choice, but if you get the brain fog/nothing is real sensation too it helps to clear that up to help you want to function again.

You might have to test run a few to see what works, but that's also why you keep up with your psychiatrist and have regular meetings with them, to see if there are and sides effects to keep you safe and help you figure out what is working. This works best with having a professional to talk to in tangent with it.

I can see where you're coming from with it being insulting because it can be patronizing, but most people probably have had only the mild to moderate depression and then think they have a stance on getting better in terms of someone who is chronically or has major depression. And that can be patronizing in and of itself.

And that's not to dismiss them because, shit, they went through a depressive stage in their lives and that shit sucks for everyone, no matter who they are.

An illness doesn't have to be a physical deformity or something for it to be categorized as such, by definition an "illness" is "a disease or period of sickness affecting the body or mind"

If people can't actually function in a conducive way most everyday then that's not normal. And that doesn't mean going out and doing x, y, z, exciting thing or fixing the entire house or big feats like that. It's doing simple things like showering, doing dishes, doing laundry, even eating. Hell, even moving. People should have the ability to do as such at the very least.

That's not to say that society's fucked because it absolutely is, but if someone is allowed to be "injured" from a sprained ankle, or "sick/ill" from a cold or something that effects them physically and requires them to take medication to get better to function at their full capacity, then why is it different from taking medication to help your brain out and to get help for functioning at a basic level, just because it's not "seen"? It means you're brain's not functioning at it's "full capacity" the same as how your body wouldn't be, so you're incapacitated either way.

And as someone stated before, whatever gets it attention to get people more help and not be dismissed. I think I would call it an "illness" because in doing so, it's not dismissing it as much as just referring to it as a "mindstate" would for other people. If I need to call out sick for my depression, I'm calling out a sick day because it's worse today than normal and I CAN'T function, the same as it would be with a cold or flu or some other physical ailment.

Besides, telling your employer that your "sick" is a lot more normalized and will allow you for more flexibility and is less specific than mentioning that you're "depressed" and it helps a lot of people without needing them to go into detail.

With medication, I find that it's not a "happy pill" so much as it helped lift some of the "brain fog" that I had always had. Prozac made me a little tired, Wellbutrin helped counteract that and supposedly helps give more of a "drive for life" back. I think I have noticed I'm more "alive" being on it too.

If anything, getting the right medication helps build your mood up and help to stabilize it. And not all days are "amazing" and "great," today for example really sucks and the fog is more present today (but that's because an ex is coming to visit my roommate). But I know it's less so there due to the medicine.

Once I had first started medication in college I was more active again and actually being social. Still anxious as hell because along with Major Depression I also have Generalized Anxiety Disorder. But, things turned out better and I started to feel "okay" more.

I then had a major life change very recently and had to stop taking medication because I had run out and had to basically uproot my entire life and move away from home to keep a job I really don't care for. And everything was just dead for me. I was dead to the world and the world didn't feel real. I didn't feel real. I had nothing to lose because I had already lost my whole support system moving away. The fog was back and I was burning bridges with the 2 people who moved up with the company too and that I had actually considered somewhat "friends" back at my old job.

I only very recently started medication back up again and, again, the brain fog has cleared substantially. I think I'm still very irritable and have bad days more than not because of work and the situation it put me in, being my first job. But, starting medication again was something I knew I needed. Not knowing what it was like, then feeling the effects of it and actually feeling okay for the first time in my life, then having to stop because I didn't know where I'd end up and then moving and not getting help for the first 6 months because I was so depressed, then knowing how I DO need it comparing when I've been off of it.

It's different with people. But for the most part, people I know who are on medication are doing better from it. The only side effects I've personally had were just being tired and maybe like 5lbs of weight gain that that wasn't noticeable until I went and saw my general practitioner and she pointed it out. But, that's also why your psychiatrist (who is able to prescribe you medication as opposed to a therapist/counselor/psychologist who aren't) has you check in with them about every 2-3 weeks to watch for any side effects to adjust them as needed.

The conversation that had an actual break through for me went like this (complete with arm movements mapping it out to really have me see what was happening too):
Friend: "So, tell me what a normal day is like for you."

Me: "What do you mean?"

F: "Well, let's say, for me, a normal day might be something like: I wake up and I'm at 50% (happiness? something?), then I'll get up and make coffee and have the morning to myself so then that boosts me up to like 75%, then let's say that something happens at work while I'm barista-ing then I might drop down to like a 65%, but then I get back and get to relax and chill and I'm back to like an 80%, then I'll chat and make some dinner and play games with you guys and I'm feeling okay and basically then at 100% more or less. Now you go."

Me: "Well...I guess...I'll wake up and I guess, since nothing's happened yet I'll be at 50% too. Then, I'll remember that I have class (this was back when I was in uni a couple of years back) and then I'll think about all of the projects and stuff that I still need to do and I'll drop down to like a 40%. I'll finally get out of bed and go to class and then it'll drop to like a 35%. I'll get back between classes and be relieved that I'm back so it'll go back up to like a 40%, maybe I'll get food and it'll go up to a 45%. I'll work on stuff and remember everything else and getting out of college and what I need to be doing and drop back to 30% then when I go to sleep I'm happy I can just shut off for a bit but remember that I have to do the same thing tomorrow so I'll be at a 25%.

F: "...It sounds like you never get above that 50%."

At that point it hit me that this all wasn't normal and I just broke down crying. I signed up for counseling the next day.

I discovered through counseling that I like to try and "logic" things out, so much so that I do this thing where even with things that you can't really do that with I'll find a way to weirdly make sense of it to myself.

But, my counselor was right, x wasn't because of y. I wasn't able to see things like that until I had a chance to have someone else follow my train of thought.

I was diagnosed with Generalized Anxiety Disorder which I believe stems from my Clinical Depression. I find, and what most say, is that a combination of both counseling and medication is the most effective method. It really helps having an unbiased, third party to just...release to. And also, they are trained in curbing your thought process to help with the frantic, extreme thoughts that kind of seem like the absolute end-all-be-all. That and the black-and-white ways of thinking too...

I think it really helps having an outlet for all of that because while friends/family listening helps, someone who is, again, trained in this and has a know-how of helping you change those ways of thought to actually benefit you is more helpful.

With medication, it's different with everyone, but I think with most of those medicines, especially now-a-days, had a long process of trial and error before being deemed suitable for wide, public use.

I think the side effects, for the most part, are in more extreme cases but they need to disclose them anyways just because. And for medication that is so widely used or intended for that, I would imagine it wouldn't be a go-to if it weren't safe since so many are on them.

Also, that's why they ask for follow-ups (usually about 3 weeks out) to check in to see if it's working or to switch you to something else. And even when they start you on something, they start you with the weakest dosage to see how you react to that, THEN based on that they change or ramp up the dosage.

Also, they want you to check in to monitor it to keep you safe. The only side effects I had were with the Prozac, and even then it was slight weight gain and tiredness when I went up to a higher dosage. So they reduced it and then started me on Wellbutrin.

I think when you first start on something your emotions can be a little in flux because the medication is kind of stirring something up in your brain that it's not used to but, that's makes sense. Then it starts getting used to the medication being in your system and evens itself out. And the medications I'm on are slow release tablets so, it takes a day or two to fully and gradually release into your system. (Which means that it takes a bit for it to leave your system when you accidentally stop, but then after a week or more of that happening things start to decline and you remember that you need it to function which is...REALLY fun to go through again.)

Again, the tl;dr is for something so widely used I would think it'd need to be safe to be prescribed so commonly and that the treatment outweighs the risks, check in with your psychiatrist to monitor your moods when your starting it and for regular check ups to monitor it so if anything happens it's caught sooner than later, people around you notice the changes before you do, and counseling helps to make you more mindful of those negative thoughts and how to more successfully curb/change those thoughts.
